title: When the problem sells itself
lines: Some businesses never need to persuade customers that the problem exists.
The pain, the embarrassment, or the deadline has already done that work.
Aspirin, Viagra, and Coffins asks what entrepreneurs should do with this uncomfortable advantage.
The book places human suffering, research, and commercial opportunity at the same table.
Its tone is ironic, but its central question is serious.
Does a business reduce vulnerability, or become more profitable by keeping it alive?
Reading it means looking at markets through the needs that polite pitch decks often hide.

title: Three signals
lines: The title introduces three market signals rather than a guide to those particular products.
Aspirin stands for a recognized problem whose relief the customer can notice.
Viagra marks intimate demand shaped by discretion, identity, and embarrassment.
Coffins point to unavoidable need when customers have little time or bargaining strength.
These signals organize an argument about urgency, trust, and the terms of exchange.
They also expose why genuine value and exploitation can appear in the same market.
The book asks readers to investigate that boundary instead of treating demand as an ethical endorsement.

title: No imaginary paradise
lines: Before examining new markets, the book challenges a convenient story about the past.
Earlier communities could provide belonging while also imposing constraint, danger, and limited privacy.
Modernity reduced many physical hardships while reorganizing work, desire, and comparison.
The historical chapters keep benefits and costs in the same account.
The factory clock is one example of technology changing the organization of daily life.
The argument is not that every earlier life was psychologically healthier.
That restraint matters when an attractive business story depends on claiming civilization has simply gone wrong.

title: Whose time is it
lines: The book follows industrial time discipline into contemporary work and digital environments.
Flexible communication can also make every hour feel available for another request.
Convenience for the sender can create a dispersed cost for the recipient.
The same arrangement may produce productivity and exhaustion at different points.
The author asks where a design choice is being mistaken for an unavoidable price of progress.
This gives readers a way to inspect the source of demand.
A product may relieve a symptom while leaving the machinery that produces it untouched.

title: Relief you can recognize
lines: The Aspirin chapter turns from metaphor to recognizable operational problems.
A person may struggle with a bill, missing documents, or coordinating care.
The need already exists without a campaign teaching customers to want it.
The commercial question becomes whether relief is observable, reliable, and worth its cost.
The book pays attention to bureaucratic friction because citizens often connect institutions manually.
A useful service can reduce repeated explanations, copied data, and uncertainty.
The deeper reading question is whether the service removes work or merely rents temporary escape from it.

title: Discretion changes demand
lines: The Viagra signal examines markets where silence hides the scale of need.
People may avoid public recommendations because a problem touches intimacy or identity.
Discretion and trustworthy access therefore become part of the service itself.
But limited public comparison can also protect ineffective or abusive offers.
The book distinguishes serving a private need from manufacturing additional shame.
Its argument concerns how incentives shape a relationship with a vulnerable customer.
That makes the chapter useful beyond the particular product named in the title.

title: The customer cannot wait
lines: The coffin chapter examines necessity under conditions of grief and unfamiliar administration.
Families may face documents, coordination, and purchases while their negotiating capacity is reduced.
The market does not need to manufacture urgency because reality already supplies it.
A service can create value through clarity, coordination, and dignified treatment.
The book also asks how opaque packages and emotional pressure can distort the transaction.
Its examples shift attention from glamorous technology to the reduction of uncertainty.
The question is whether the business helps a family through the situation or exploits its constraints.

title: An exception in every window
lines: The discussion of social media keeps its genuine benefits in view.
Rare communities, distant relationships, learning, and publication all matter to the argument.
The concern is how comparison and retention incentives can interact with vulnerability.
The book reviews an uneven evidence base rather than declaring one simple universal effect.
Average associations cannot describe every user, context, or pattern of use.
That caution interrupts the easy story a technology critic might prefer to sell.
The chapter asks which mechanisms deserve investigation and what a user can actually control.

title: The same friendly interface
lines: Conversational AI sharpens the question because several different services can look like a conversation.
The book separates administration, clinical assistance, structured interventions, and general companionship.
Their responsibilities do not become equivalent because they share a friendly interface.
A system that reduces paperwork has different obligations from one addressing vulnerable people.
The discussion asks what evidence, supervision, and accountability match each role.
It also examines the tension between helping a person and maximizing continued interaction.
Read this chapter for those distinctions, rather than a blanket promise or rejection of conversational AI.

title: Work nobody photographs
lines: The atlas of unpleasant industries expands the argument beyond emotional technology.
Care coordination, sanitation, maintenance, compliance, and other difficult work can carry persistent unmet needs.
These markets may demand operational patience rather than an elegant digital demonstration.
The book does not assume that an unglamorous industry is automatically profitable.
Regulation, procurement, trust, and weak margins can still make execution difficult.
Its challenge is to stop using a founder’s social discomfort as a market filter.
The reader is invited to stay close enough to a problem to understand who actually bears it.

title: A market or a colony
lines: Psychological distress raises the book’s most uncomfortable commercial question.
Greater recognition and inadequate services can make a real need more visible.
Technology might reduce barriers while also creating new ways to monetize dependence.
The difference depends partly on what a company counts as success.
Longer use can mean value in one setting and unresolved vulnerability in another.
The book asks whether users can leave more autonomous than they arrived.
That question connects its market analysis to the ethics of product architecture.

title: Can the business survive success
lines: Suppose a product worked so well that its customers needed it less often.
Would the business remain viable under its own definition of success?
The ethics chapter places that test inside pricing, design, and operational decisions.
It rejects the idea that responsibility can be added after growth as a decorative policy.
A good intention cannot repair incentives that reward maintaining the original problem.
The reader gains a way to examine promises against the arrangement that pays for them.
The chapter develops this tension without treating profit itself as the enemy.

title: Keep the dentist
lines: The closing argument calls for a selective relationship with modern life.
It preserves medicine, knowledge, freedom, and productive capacity while questioning avoidable costs.
The proposed direction is redesign, rather than a romantic retreat into the past.
The prediction chapter also asks readers to distinguish evidence from a persuasive scenario.
What matters is what can be measured before a compelling story becomes infrastructure.
The book reserves its practical depth for designs, organizations, and markets with better aligned incentives.
Its irony makes room for a serious account of what improvement would require.

title: Follow the bill
lines: This is a book for readers willing to examine opportunity without sterilizing its human context.
Its distinctive perspective connects obvious demand with the vulnerability that gives demand its force.
The historical chapters explain how those needs change rather than simply disappear.
The market chapters offer signals, while the ethics chapters question what responding well would mean.
Begin with the prologue, then compare the Aspirin signal with the test of customer autonomy.
Follow the benefits, but also follow where the costs and dependencies land.
That is the reading invitation behind Aspirin, Viagra, and Coffins.
